newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Hopes rise for S.African markets after dismal 1996.
newsitem.headline: Hopes rise for S.African markets after dismal 1996.

text.p: After a dismal 1996, hopes are reviving that South Africa will deliver its potential as an emerging market in 1997, analysts said on Thursday.

Markets have made a good start, with long bond yields falling some 50 basis points to the best levels in three months, and share prices tracking a worldwide equities rally despite a meltdown in the gold price.
Bond traders say foreigners are the key to recent strength: non-residents put a net 635 million rand ($136 million) into South African bonds in the first three days of this week alone.
Offshore, Eurorand issues are back in fashion as investors roll over their exposure to the South African currency.
Underpinning it is a belief that the rand will stabilise in 1997, depreciating only in line with inflation differentials, after falling 29 percent against the dollar last year.
"Unlike last year, an environment characterised by more positive than negative...factors can be expected to impact on the rand in 1997," Standard Bank's Economics Division said.

It sees an average rand/dollar rate of 4.72 in the first quarter, slipping to 4.90 in the fourth -- a prediction broadly in line with the views of other economists polled by Reuters at the end of last year. The rand is currently around 4.65.

Constantin Vayenas, emerging markets analyst at UBS in London, says South Africa should be a recovery story in 1997 with the weaker rand boosting the trade balance and foreign inflows reviving, lifting reserves from current critical levels.
Last year South Africa had a current account deficit of $2.5 billion of which $2.1 billion had to be funded by the Reserve Bank, slashing reserves to less than four weeks' import cover.
But this year the current account deficit should narrow to $1.6 billion, as imports slow and exports get a currency fillip, while net foreign inflows should hit $3.4 billion, Vayenas said.
That would lift official gold and foreign exchange reserves back to $4.0 billion by year-end from December's $2.2 billion.
"Despite the fact that 1997 is not going to be a good growth year, the fundamental picture is improving," Vayenas said.
Most economists expect GDP growth to slow to little more than two percent in 1997 from three percent in 1996.
Noises from African National Congress politicians have also been largely encouraging -- despite this week's diplomatic spat with the U.S. over arm sales to Syria.

The privatisation drive appears to be back on track with Public Enterprises Minister Stella Sigcau spelling out that four public sector corporations will be sold outright in 1997 and strategic equity partners found for a further three.

Most attention is focused on the sale of up to 30 percent in Telkom by April. That deal, which is expected to value the telecommunications concern at over $4.0 billion, will be sub-Saharan Africa's largest privatisation.
Peter Worthington of J.P. Morgan said privatisation could play a key role in a steadier rand and firmer markets in 1997.

"For 1997, I would look for greater rand stability -- the fundamentals should certainly support that with the turnaround in the trade account and more long-term capital inflows through direct investment and privatisation," he said.
Confidence is also growing that Finance Minister Trevor Manuel will deliver hoped-for fiscal discipline in his March 12 budget which may also see some cautious easing of exchange controls.
Manuel said recently he was preparing real spending cuts to ensure the deficit reached the target in 1997/98.
"(The budget) is likely to feature a tight grip on expenditure, no increase in the overall tax burden and a firm deficit-to-GDP target of four percent," Standard Bank predicted.
Gold's descent to three-year lows may take the shine off the mining sector's export performance. But South Africa's exposure to gold is much less than in the past.
In the last 10 years, gold's contribution to South Africa's total export earnings has virtually halved from 42.5 percent in 1986 to 23.1 percent in 1995, according to the Minerals Bureau.
The mining industry as a whole contributed only 7.7 percent to GDP in 1995, down from 15.4 percent in 1986, and gold's share of that was less than half.
